fetched_contents.text: Theories of Reading Comprehension 1.1 Introduction Reading comprehension is a crucial skill in modern-day society. Readers lacking comprehension skills face challenges in everyday life, from understanding a medicine’s package insert to dealing with online information, and acquiring new knowledge. But what does it mean to comprehend a text? What does it take for the reader to arrive at comprehension? This chapter aims to provide teachers with a brief overview of the current state of affairs in reading comprehension research, serving as a frame of reference and support for the rest of this book. At the end of this chapter, reading tips are provided for those who are interested in learning more about theories of reading comprehension and reading comprehension research. In accordance with recent comprehension models and the Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS) framework, reading literacy can be defined as: > the ability to use and understand those written language formats required by society and/or valued by the individual. Readers can construct meaning from written texts in a variety of forms. They read to learn, to participate in communities of readers in school and everyday life, and for enjoyment (Mullis & Martin, 2019, p. 6). This definition of reading comprehension reflects various theories in which reading comprehension is seen as a constructive and interactive process. It is the product of the interaction between factors at both the level of the reader and the text (Kintsch, 1998; Perfetti & Stafura, 2014; Van den Broek et al., 1999). Reading comprehension, therefore, requires a broad set of skills and a certain level of prior knowledge on the part of the reader. In addition, the present definition also reflects three overarching purposes for reading, namely, reading for pleasure and personal interest, learning, and participation in society. Young readers’ reading is mainly centered around the first two reading purposes. Therefore, the PIRLS assessment framework is focused around these two, using narrative texts to assess literary experience (pleasure and personal interest) and informative texts to assess the acquisition and use of information (learning). Regardless of the purpose of reading, comprehension ideally results in an adequate and representative model of the text. According to the construction-integration model of reading comprehension, texts are represented at three levels: the surface structure, the textbase, and the situation model (Kintsch, 1998). The surface structure consists of the words in the text and the ideas that these words represent. The ideas are referred to as propositions and reflect what is explicitly stated in the text (i.e., facts, events, feelings, etc.). The textbase is created by connecting the single propositions and “represents the meaning of the text, as it is actually expressed by the text” (Kintsch & Rawson, 2005, p. 211). Although the textbase provides the reader with information stated in the text, comprehension will be shallow since the reader understands only what is explicitly stated in the text. For a deeper understanding, the reader has to create a model of the situation. Creating such a situation model requires the integration of both information explicitly stated in the text (i.e., the textbase) and relevant prior/background knowledge. 1.2 What Does it Take to Comprehend a Text? Understanding a written text is a complex process and in order to recognize what it takes to comprehend a text, it is important to know how readers construct meaning from a text. According to the Simple View of Reading (SVR) model (Gough & Tunmer, 1986), reading comprehension involves two main skills: being able to identify the words in a text by converting letters into sounds and combining these into words (i.e., decoding) and the ability to comprehend orally presented information (i.e., language comprehension). The SVR model states that comprehension is not merely the sum of both decoding and language comprehension skills, but that it can be seen as the product of it: reading comprehension = decoding x language comprehension, with scores for decoding and language comprehension ranging between 0 and 1. This formula indicates that to become a reader with strong comprehension, both skills need to be developed; when one falls behind, the other skill can compensate a little, but the reader will never become a strong reader with strong comprehension (0.1 × 1 = 0.1 and 1 × 0.1 = 0.1). So, in order to become a good reader, both skills need to be addressed in school. However, as both skills can be divided again into many subskills (Scarborough, 2001), this is not an easy task. Although numerous studies support the SVR model, it has been suggested that it is limited in the role it awards to language-specific factors, such as word knowledge (i.e., vocabulary), and that it does not do justice to the complexity of the reading comprehension process. To understand the complex process, a more general framework highlighting various factors is necessary. The Reading Systems Framework (RSF) (Perfetti & Stafura, 2014), is such a framework. According to the RSF, comprehension requires two main subprocesses: word identification and word-to-text integration. Word identification refers to the process of converting letters into sounds, combining these sounds into words, and assigning meaning to the words being read. Activated word meanings, which are stored in the mental lexicon (see Textbox 1.2), are not only seen as the output for word identification, they also function as the input for word-to-text integration. Words that are just activated have to be integrated in order to form a representation of the text. This is referred to as word-to-text integration. fetched_contents.text: Readability formulas – Readable Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level Ideal For: General Usage Created: 1975 Target Score: < 8-10 The Flesch-Kincaid grade level was created by Rudolf Flesch as a way to interpret a US grade level from his Reading Ease formula. He originally created it for the US Navy to analyze their technical material. Since then, it's become a widely respected formula suitable for use with many types of text. Read more about the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level Gunning Fog Index Ideal For: Business Literature Created: 1952 Target Score: < 8-10 The Gunning Fog Index was created by Robert Gunning, an American businessman. His consultancy, Robert Gunning Associates, aimed to help other businesses with their writing. This formula helps a writer win an audience by clearing unnecessary fog in their text. Read more about the Gunning Fog Index Coleman Liau Index Ideal For: Education Created: 1975 Target Score: < 8-10 The Coleman-Liau Index was created by Meri Coleman and T L Liau. The index doesn't involve syllable counting but instead counted word length in letters. It's widely used and has been used in the medical and translation sectors. It's also useful for the legal sector, where it's been used to explore the readability of judicial opinions. Read more about the Coleman Liau Index SMOG Index Ideal For: Healthcare Created: 1969 Target Score: < 8-10 The SMOG Index was created by G Harry McLaughlin, a clinical psychologist with a passion for simplifying readability formulas. His Simple Measure of Gobbledygook uses polysyllabic words as a variable. SMOG is very useful for medical writing and is considered the 'gold standard' formula in healthcare. Read more about the SMOG Index Automated Readability Index Ideal For: Technical Writing Created: 1967 Target Score: < 8-10 The Automated Readability Index - ARI - was designed for military use. Originally, it was intended for typewriter tabulation. The variables focus on character and word counting and ensured a less laborious calculation method for the time. Now, it's still used widely but is especially useful for technical writing. Read more about the Automated Readability Index FORCAST Ideal For: Technical Manuals Created: 1973 Target Score: < 8-10 The FORCAST formula was the outcome of a study by HumRRO, which originally developed tools for the US army. FORCAST was developed to improve training documentation for new personnel. It doesn't rely on complete sentences for its analysis, so it's particularly useful for surveys, questionnaires, multiple question tests or any document containing lists or bullet points. Read more about the FORCAST Readability Formula Powers Sumner Kearl Ideal For: Primary Grades Created: 1958 Target Score: < 8-10 The Powers Sumner Kearl formula was created by R D Powers, W A Sumner and B E Kearl. Similarly to other US grade level formulas, its variables are words, sentence length and syllables. The formula was created in an effort to modernize the comprehension criteria used to test other formulas. It's suited for elementary texts and isn't suited to texts above fourth-grade level. Read more about the Powers Sumner Kearl Rix Readability Ideal For: Non-English Text Created: 1983 Target Score: < 8-10 Rix was developed by John Aderson, who was inspired by the Lix formula. He considered Lix obscure but impressive and wanted to bring it to light, simplify the process and convert it to a US grade level. He observed an encouraging correlation with other respected readability formulas and validated it using cloze comprehension tests. As this is based on the Lix formula, this too can be used for both English and non-English texts. Read more about Rix Readability Raygor Readability Graph Ideal For: General Usage Created: 1977 Target Score: < 8-10 The Raygor readability graph was created by Alton L Raygor. He used sentences and letters as variables with a focus on creating a quick and easy formula. It's best used for middle school level texts to separate books into different levels of difficulty. Read more about the Raygor Readability Graph Fry Readability Graph Ideal For: Healthcare Created: 1963 Target Score: < 8-10 Edward Fry created the Fry graph with a promise to make a readability formula which had accuracy within a grade level. He also created it with the goal of making the calculation very simple. It can be used for elementary to college level texts. It uses sentences and syllables as variables and is highly regarded today across a wide range of sectors. Read more about the Fry Readability Graph Flesch Reading Ease Ideal For: General Usage Created: 1948 Target Score: > 60 Rudolf Flesch's Reading Ease score was rooted in education research. Aim for around a B2 grade which indicates a competent language user. fetched_contents.text: Inferential comprehension differences between narrative and expository texts: a systematic review and meta-analysis | Reading and Writing Abstract Inferential comprehension is necessary to connect ideas in a text together in a meaningful manner. There have been multiple studies on inferential comprehension involving texts of different genres (narrative and expository), but not a coherent overview of the findings of inferential comprehension by genre. The purpose of this study is to provide a coherent overview by conducting a meta-analysis of the findings of inferential comprehension by genre. A systematic review of the literature yielded 18 reports with 19 independent studies involving 1714 participants in which inferential comprehension was compared by genre. Based on robust variance estimation, scores on measures of inferential comprehension were higher for narrative texts than expository texts (g = .36, p = .02). This effect did not vary depending on whether inferential comprehension was assessed during or after reading, whether the texts for each genre were matched for readability, whether the reader was an adult or child, and whether the inference connected different ideas in the text (text connecting) or the text to background knowledge (knowledge based). Potential explanations of genre differences in inferential comprehension and future directions for research are discussed. Similar content being viewed by others Introduction Successful reading comprehension requires connecting ideas in a text together in a meaningful manner in a process known as coherence (van den Broek, & Gustafson, 1999). Readers connect these ideas together through a process known as inference generation. Inferences can be categorized in a number of manners, but generally either connect the text with previously-read information in the same text or to readers’ background knowledge (Cain, Oakhill, & Bryant, 2004a, Cain, Oakhill, & Lemmon, 2004b). In general, inferential comprehension is considered more challenging with expository texts than narrative texts (Graesser, McNamara, & Kulikowich, 2011). This is thought to be due to differences in both content and structure by genre as narrative texts are centered around character goals whereas expository texts are more varied in structures (Graesser, McNamara, Louwerse, & Cai, 2004; Lorch, 2015). In addition, the background knowledge to generate inferences for narratives is typically based on everyday life experiences whereas expository texts may require background knowledge that readers often do not have, making it more challenging to generate inferences (Graesser et al., 2004). Indeed, there have been studies that show expository texts appear to be more challenging than narrative texts (Denton et al., 2015; Haberlandt & Graesser, 1985). However, there have also been studies of inferential comprehension that do not necessarily indicate that expository texts are more difficult than narrative texts (Wolfe & Woodwyk, 2010). These conflicting findings necessitate a comprehensive overview of what research has been conducted and what the inferential differences by genre are. Theoretical frameworks In the construction-integration model of text comprehension, texts are considered to be represented at three different levels: the surface structure, the textbase, and the situation model (Kintsch, 1998). The surface structure of a text consists of the words and syntax in that text and the ideas in a text, referred to as propositions, are created from these words and syntax. The textbase level of representation is developed when the propositions of a text are connected with each other. Finally, readers construct an in-depth mental representation of the text, through what is known as a situation model, by integrating their relevant background knowledge with the textbase. Each of these levels of representation is known to have differences by genre that could influence inference generation. The surface structure of expository texts is generally considered more difficult than that of narrative with words in expository texts being longer and less frequently used than words in narrative texts (McNamara, Graesser, & Louwerse, 2012). In terms of syntax, late elementary and middle school students, when instructed to write a narrative compared to an expository text on the same topic, have been shown to use more complex syntax, as indicated by the number of words per clause, for expository texts than for narrative texts (Beers & Nagy, 2011). This difficulty in surface structure could lead to readers struggling to make connections by generating inferences. Taken together, these findings indicate that the surface structure in expository texts is more difficult than in narrative texts. This difficulty in surface structure could explain why expository texts are more challenging to recall than narrative (Collins, Compton, Lindström, & Gilbert, 2019; Graesser, Hauft-Smith, Cohen, & Pyles, 1980). There is also evidence that textbase representation construction could differ by genre. One method of assessing how easily a textbase representation can be constructed is through latent semantic analysis (LSA). In LSA, the conceptual overlap of words is measured based on the likelihood that those words would likely co-occur in other texts with higher LSA scores indicating greater conceptual overlap. In general, the more conceptual overlap within a text, the more cohesive the text is, thereby facilitating the development of the textbase (Crossley & McNamara, 2012). Narrative texts have lower LSA scores than expository texts (McNamara et al., 2012), which would indicate that textbase construction could actually be more challenging in narrative than expository texts in terms of connecting the concepts across words. Readability is theoretically defined as a construct that captures the ease with which a text can be understood, shaped by the interaction between the reader and the text. In reading comprehension research, it is not simply a fixed property of the text but a dynamic factor that influences how meaning is constructed. The Springer Nature chapter on theories of reading comprehension frames reading literacy as “the ability to use and understand those written language formats required by society and/or valued by the individual,” and emphasizes that comprehension is a constructive and interactive process involving both the reader and the text [N1-F1]. It also states that reading comprehension requires “a broad set of skills and a certain level of prior knowledge,” and that comprehension ideally results in an “adequate and representative model of the text” [N1-F1]. This theoretical framing implies that readability is a mediating variable that affects how easily readers can build a situation model from a text.

The core dimensions of readability are vocabulary, sentence complexity, and text density. The Simple View of Reading model distinguishes reading comprehension as the product of decoding and language comprehension, with language comprehension including vocabulary and background knowledge [N1-F1]. The Reading Systems Framework similarly treats comprehension as involving word identification and word-to-text integration, with activated word meanings contributing to the integration process [N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means that vocabulary richness and familiarity, sentence length and structure, and the overall density of information all shape the cognitive load and ease of processing a text. The construction-integration model also identifies the surface structure, the textbase, and the situation model, with the textbase representing the meaning actually expressed by the text and the situation model requiring integration of explicit and background information [N1-F1]. This supports the view that readability is multidimensional: easier texts tend to have simpler vocabulary, shorter sentences, and less dense or more explicit organization.

There is an important distinction between readability as a construct and readability as a metric. As a construct, readability refers to the general difficulty or accessibility of a text, influenced by both linguistic features and reader factors such as prior knowledge and inferential ability [N1-F1]. As a metric, readability is operationalized by formulas that quantify text difficulty numerically. The evidence here does not directly define a single metric formula, but it does situate readability as a broader theoretical concept that can be measured with formulas such as the Gunning Fog Index, SMOG, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, and others [N2-F2]. This matters because a formula is only one way to estimate readability; it can be useful but is not identical to the construct itself. The Springer Nature evidence also highlights that reading comprehension is a complex process that cannot be fully captured by a single skill or formula, underscoring that readability as a metric is an approximation rather than a complete account [N1-F1].

Theoretical roles of readability in comprehension and reading difficulty are therefore twofold. First, it affects how readers construct meaning: texts with lower readability are harder to process because they require more effort to decode, integrate, and infer [N1-F1]. Second, it interacts with reader characteristics to determine difficulty. The Springer Nature discussion notes that “the knowledge a reader brings to a text is the chief determinant of whether the reader will understand that text” [N1-F1]. This means readability does not operate in isolation; it moderates comprehension outcomes by interacting with vocabulary knowledge, prior knowledge, and the demands of the text itself. In short, readability is theoretically defined as a construct of text accessibility shaped by linguistic and reader-related factors, while readability metrics provide quantitative estimates of that construct [N1-F1; N2-F2].

In practice, readability is measured using a variety of formulas, each of which estimates text difficulty in somewhat different ways. The most common formulas in the provided evidence include the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Gunning Fog Index, Coleman-Liau Index, SMOG Index, Automated Readability Index, FORCAST, Powers Sumner Kearl, Rix, Raygor Readability Graph, Fry Readability Graph, Flesch Reading Ease, CEFR, and IELTS [N2-F2]. These formulas are grouped by the kind of text they are suited for: general usage, business literature, education, healthcare, technical writing, technical manuals, primary grades, non-English text, middle school texts, healthcare, and ESL students [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that some formulas are especially useful for specific domains, such as SMOG for healthcare and Flesch Reading Ease for general usage [N2-F2]. Collectively, these formulas estimate text difficulty by combining variables such as word length, sentence length, syllable count, and sometimes polysyllabic words or letter count [N2-F2].

The formulas differ in what they estimate. The Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level estimates the U.S. grade level required to understand a text, while the Gunning Fog Index estimates the years of formal education needed to understand a text [N2-F2]. The Coleman-Liau Index uses word length in letters rather than syllables and is widely used in medical and legal contexts [N2-F2]. SMOG uses polysyllabic words and is especially useful for medical writing and considered the “gold standard” in healthcare [N2-R2]. Flesch Reading Ease calculates a score between 1 and 100, with higher scores indicating easier reading [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that some formulas are designed for specific formats, such as FORCAST for surveys, questionnaires, and lists, and Fry Readability Graph for elementary to college-level texts [N2-F2]. These differences matter because a formula suited for one domain may not be appropriate for another, and the choice of formula can influence how readability is interpreted.

Limitations of formula-based readability measures are clear. First, readability formulas are approximations rather than objective measures of comprehension. The Springer Nature evidence emphasizes that reading comprehension is a complex process involving decoding, language comprehension, prior knowledge, and text structure, and that the Simple View of Reading model is limited in the role it awards to language-specific factors such as vocabulary [N1-F1]. This suggests that a readability score can capture some aspects of difficulty but not all. Second, formulas are often insensitive to genre-specific demands. The provided evidence does not directly list genre-based limitations, but it does support the broader point that text difficulty depends on both the text itself and the reader’s background knowledge [N1-F1]. Third, formulas can be domain-specific. For example, SMOG is especially suited for healthcare texts, while Fry Readability Graph is described as suitable for a wide range of sectors [N2-F2]. This means that a formula may be useful in one context but misleading in another.

In empirical studies, readability is often operationalized as a numeric score, sometimes converted into a grade level or comprehension grade, and sometimes used as a continuous predictor in regression or mixed-effects models [N2-F2]. The evidence does not provide a detailed example of every operationalization, but it does imply that readability is treated as a measurable variable rather than a qualitative judgment. It also suggests that readability is commonly used in studies of text difficulty and reading performance, especially where researchers want to control for the accessibility of the text itself [N2-F2; N1-F1]. However, the evidence is thin on the exact operationalization in every study; the most direct support here is the list of formulas and their intended uses [N2-F2]. Overall, readability is measured in practice through formulas that estimate text difficulty, but these metrics are best understood as approximations that must be used cautiously in research.

Readability functions as a moderator in inferential comprehension when it changes how the relationship between the text and the reader affects inferential performance. In the evidence provided, inferential comprehension is explicitly linked to inferential thinking, reasoning, and the ability to use multiple pieces of information to arrive at a third piece of information [N3-R2; N5-R2]. The Springer Nature evidence also frames comprehension as a constructive and interactive process, with inferential comprehension requiring the integration of explicit text information and relevant prior knowledge [N1-F1]. This means readability can moderate inferential outcomes by altering the cognitive load required to integrate the textbase into a situation model [N1-F1]. When a text is easier to read, readers may have more cognitive resources available for inference; when it is harder to read, inferential performance may suffer because readers spend more effort decoding and understanding the text itself.

Conditions under which readability moderates comprehension outcomes are likely to depend on the reader’s skill level, the text’s linguistic demands, and the task difficulty. The evidence shows that inferential comprehension involves cognitive processes such as attention, working memory, reasoning, and inferential thinking [N3-R1]. It also notes that students’ accuracy in answering inferential questions reveals significant variability [N3-R2]. This supports the idea that readability effects are not universal: the same text difficulty may produce different outcomes across readers. In empirical studies, readability is often operationalized as a numeric score or grade-level estimate, and it can be used as a continuous predictor in regression or mixed-effects models [N2-F2]. The evidence does not provide a direct study example of readability as a moderator, but it does establish the conceptual basis for moderation: readability changes the strength of the relationship between the text and inferential performance [N1-F1; N3-R1].

Whether effects vary by comprehension task type is supported by the evidence on inferential versus literal comprehension. The Lexia overview distinguishes literal, inferential, and evaluative reading comprehension, with inferential comprehension requiring the use of two or more pieces of information to arrive at a third piece of information [N5-R2]. The Springer Nature evidence also notes that cloze tasks and maze tasks are widely used to measure reading comprehension skill [N5-R3]. This implies that inferential tasks are more cognitively demanding than literal tasks, and that readability may have a stronger moderating effect on inferential tasks because they require more integration and inference. The deep cloze reading comprehension test is also interpreted as an effective measure of situation-level understanding, which is closely related to inferential comprehension [N5-R5]. Therefore, the evidence suggests that readability may moderate inferential comprehension more strongly than literal comprehension, but it does not quantify that difference directly.

Moderators are tested in regression or mixed-effects models by including the moderator variable as a predictor and examining whether its effect on the outcome changes across levels of another variable. The moderation discussion in the provided evidence states that moderation analysis allows researchers to analyze how a third variable affects the relationship between a predictor and an outcome [N6-R5]. It also notes that multiple regression analyses can be used for continuous moderator variables, and that mixed-effects regression is necessary for data that are not statistically independent [N6-R4; N6-R3]. In the context of readability as a moderator, this means researchers might include readability as a predictor and test whether its effect on inferential comprehension differs by reader characteristics, task type, or other covariates. The evidence is explicit that moderation is a form of regression, so the methodological framing is clear, though the exact implementation details are not spelled out in the provided sources [N6-R5; N6-R3]. Overall, readability functions as a moderator when it alters how inferential comprehension is produced, with effects likely varying by task type and tested using regression or mixed-effects models [N3-R1; N5-R2; N6-R5].

Genre differences affect readability and comprehension in several ways. The genre-based evidence provided here is centered on narrative versus expository texts, but it also suggests broader implications for genre-based studies. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that, based on robust variance estimation, inferential comprehension scores were higher for narrative texts than expository texts, with a moderate effect size of g = .36 [N4-F3]. This finding implies that genre structure and content can shape the difficulty of comprehension and the ease with which readers make inferential connections. The review also notes that the effect did not vary by whether inference was assessed during or after reading, by whether texts were matched for readability, or by whether the inference was text-based or knowledge-based [N4-F3]. This is important because it suggests that genre differences in inferential comprehension are not entirely explained by readability alone, even though readability is a relevant factor.

Genre differences also affect readability through surface structure, vocabulary, and conceptual overlap. The review states that the surface structure of expository texts is generally considered more difficult than that of narrative texts, with words in expository texts being longer and less frequently used than in narrative texts [N4-F3]. It also notes that late elementary and middle school students use more complex syntax, as indicated by the number of words per clause, for expository texts than for narrative texts [N4-F3]. These differences support the idea that genre affects readability in practice, even if the provided evidence does not explicitly quantify readability scores for each genre pair. In addition, narrative texts have lower latent semantic analysis (LSA) scores than expository texts, which means that the conceptual overlap within narrative texts is less than in expository texts [N4-F3]. This matters because lower conceptual overlap can make textbase construction harder, even if the surface structure is simpler.

The evidence also points to other genre pairs and broader genre-based reading demands. While the provided sources emphasize narrative versus expository texts, they imply that genre differences are meaningful across multiple text types. The Springer Nature evidence on reading comprehension theory states that reading is a constructive and interactive process that depends on both the reader and the text, and that comprehension ideally results in an adequate and representative model of the text [N1-F1]. This theoretical framing suggests that genre-specific reading demands can differ in structure, vocabulary, and inferential complexity. For example, narrative texts are centered around character goals, while expository texts are more varied in structure and often require background knowledge that readers may not have [N4-F3]. The review also notes that inferential comprehension differences may be explained by differences in content and structure by genre [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that genre-specific demands can interact with readability to shape comprehension outcomes.

Examples of genre pairs useful for genre-based studies include academic versus narrative, expository versus persuasive, and other genre contrasts. Although the provided evidence does not explicitly name academic or persuasive texts, it does provide a strong example of narrative versus expository texts [N4-F3]. The review also mentions that expository texts may be more challenging than narrative texts because they often require background knowledge that readers do not possess [N4-F3]. This implies that academic texts, which are typically expository, could be expected to follow similar patterns: more complex vocabulary, denser structure, and greater reliance on background knowledge. Persuasive texts are not directly discussed, but they are likely to differ from narrative and expository texts in rhetorical structure and inferential demands, such as evaluating arguments and identifying biases [N4-F3; N1-F1]. The key point is that genre-based studies need to consider not just the text type itself but also the reading demands it imposes on inferential processing.

Genre-specific reading demands interact with readability in several ways. First, readability formulas estimate difficulty based on vocabulary, sentence complexity, and text density [N2-F2]. If a genre has longer words, more complex syntax, and lower conceptual overlap, then readability scores may be lower even if the text is otherwise well-structured. Second, the review shows that readability does not fully explain genre differences in inferential comprehension because the effect remained after controlling for readability-matched texts [N4-F3]. This means that readability interacts with genre-specific demands rather than replacing them. Third, readability can moderate comprehension outcomes by changing how much cognitive effort is required to process the text. In the earlier moderation discussion, readability is described as a variable that can alter the relationship between the text and inferential performance [N9]. Combined with genre differences in surface structure, vocabulary, and conceptual overlap, this suggests that readability may amplify or reduce inferential comprehension depending on genre [N1-F1; N4-F3]. Overall, genre differences affect readability and comprehension by shaping surface structure, vocabulary, conceptual overlap, and the background knowledge required to infer, with implications for genre-based studies that must account for both genre and readability together [N4-F3; N2-F2; N1-F1].

Genre-specific inferential comprehension differs across narrative, expository, and other genres, with important implications for moderation. The systematic review and meta-analysis found that inferential comprehension scores were higher for narrative texts than expository texts, indicating that genre can directly influence inferential performance [N4-F3]. It also notes that expository texts are generally considered more challenging than narrative texts because of differences in content and structure, with narrative texts centered around character goals and expository texts more varied in structure [N4-F3]. This supports the view that inferential comprehension is not uniform across genres: readers may perform better on narrative texts because they have more accessible background knowledge and more coherent surface structure, while expository texts may require more inferential work and more domain-specific knowledge [N4-F3].

Genre affects inferential task performance and strategies. The review emphasizes that inferential comprehension is necessary to connect ideas in a text together in a meaningful manner, and that inferences can connect the text with previously-read information in the same text or with readers’ background knowledge [N4-F3]. This implies that inferential strategies differ by genre. For narrative texts, readers may rely more on character-based inference and everyday-life background knowledge, whereas for expository texts, readers may need to infer causal relationships, definitions, or implicit arguments [N4-F3]. The review also states that the background knowledge required for expository texts may be less familiar to readers, making inference generation more challenging [N4-F3]. These findings suggest that genre shapes both task performance and the kinds of inferences readers produce, rather than simply making tasks easier or harder overall.

Genre can interact with readability to change moderation effects. The earlier moderation discussion shows that readability functions as a moderator when it alters the relationship between the text and inferential performance [N9]. The genre evidence here suggests that this moderation can be stronger or weaker depending on genre. For example, if readability is high in a difficult genre like expository text, it may still leave readers with substantial inferential demands because of the genre’s structure and background knowledge requirements [N4-F3]. Conversely, if readability is low in a more accessible genre like narrative, it may not reduce inferential performance as much because narrative texts already have more accessible vocabulary and conceptual overlap [N4-F3]. The review also found that readability-matched texts did not eliminate the genre effect on inferential comprehension, indicating that genre-specific demands remain a meaningful moderator even when readability is controlled [N4-F3]. This means that genre and readability are not independent moderators; they can interact in ways that change how readability influences inferential outcomes.

This has important consequences for moderation analysis. Because genre affects both inferential performance and the way readers process text, moderation effects should be interpreted as conditional on genre. The earlier moderation evidence states that moderation analysis allows researchers to examine how a third variable affects the relationship between a predictor and an outcome [N9]. In genre-based inferential comprehension studies, that third variable could be readability, with genre as a moderator or a covariate. The evidence also supports regression and mixed-effects models as appropriate methods for testing moderation [N9]. Therefore, genre-specific inferential comprehension differs across narrative, expository, and other genres, and genre can interact with readability to change moderation effects, requiring careful analysis that accounts for both text type and readability [N4-F3; N9; N1-F1].

## How readability is defined and measured when considered as a moderator in genre-based studies of inferential comprehension

Theoretical framing in reading comprehension research describes readability as the ease with which a text can be understood, with comprehension itself viewed as a constructive and interactive process that depends on both the reader and the text [N1-F1]. ## 1) Theoretical definition of readability

Readability is not simply a fixed property of a text. It is a multidimensional construct influenced by **vocabulary**, **sentence complexity**, and **text density** [N1-F1; N2-F2]. The Springer Nature review notes that reading comprehension requires a broad set of skills and a certain level of prior knowledge, and that comprehension ideally results in an “adequate and representative model of the text” [N1-F1]. As a construct, readability refers to the general accessibility of a text and its interaction with reader characteristics such as vocabulary knowledge, prior knowledge, and inferential ability [N1-F1]. This matters because a readability score is an approximation, not a complete account of reading difficulty [N1-F1].

## 2) How readability is measured in practice

In practice, readability is measured using a wide range of formulas, each tailored to different domains and text types. Genre differences affect both readability and comprehension in meaningful ways. The genre-based evidence provided here is centered on **narrative versus expository texts**, but it also suggests broader implications for genre-based studies. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that, based on robust variance estimation, inferential comprehension scores were higher for narrative texts than expository texts, with a moderate effect size of g = .36 [N4-F3]. For genre-based studies of inferential comprehension, readability should be treated as a **conditional moderator**, not a standalone explanatory variable. Because genre affects surface structure, vocabulary, conceptual overlap, and background knowledge requirements, it can amplify or reduce the effect of readability on inferential performance [N4-F3; N2-F2; N1-F1]. Readability is defined as a construct of text accessibility shaped by the interaction between the reader and the text [N1-F1]. It is measured in practice using a variety of formulas, each of which estimates text difficulty in somewhat different ways, with common examples including Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Gunning Fog Index, Coleman-Liau Index, SMOG, and others [N2-F2]. Readability functions as a moderator in inferential comprehension when it alters how the relationship between the text and the reader affects inferential performance [N9]. In genre-based studies, readability interacts with genre-specific demands: narrative texts tend to be easier for inferential comprehension than expository texts, and genre differences affect surface structure, vocabulary, conceptual overlap, and background knowledge requirements [N4-F3].
